newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Air New Zealand shoots for the sky with Ansett deal.
newsitem.headline: Air New Zealand shoots for the sky with Ansett deal.

text.p: Air New Zealand has shot for the sky in its bid to buy half of Ansett Holdings, Managing Director Jim McCrea said on Tuesday.
The transaction will double assets to NZ$6.9 billion (US$4.75 billion) and make it a serious contender in the regional aviation market.
McCrea was ecstatic that the deal, two years in the making, was coming to fruition.

"I'm delighted to say that after a substantial period of aero-political development and evolution ... we are now able to say that we are about to acquire a 50 percent interest in Ansett Australia," McCrea told a news conference on Tuesday.
"It has not sunk in. It's been going on for such a long time," McCrea said.
The NZ$540 million deal to by TNT Ltd's half share must be approved by Air NZ shareholders on September 27.
Brierley Investments, which holds 42 percent of Air NZ, supports the transaction.
Air NZ's and Ansett's main rival, Qantas Airways, holds 19.9 percent of Air NZ, and may play a spoiling role.
The deal is also subject to approval from the Australia Foreign Investment Review Board, due to decide by September 26.

Part of the plan involves Rupert Mudoch's News Corp, Ansett's other half-owner, buying Ansett New Zealand to meet the New Zealand Commerce Commission's concerns that domestic competition be maintained.
McCrea said it was an appropriate step in the evolution of the single aviation market with Australia and that it could hasten progress towards that goal.

"On the basis of the investment, we have created a very, very strong regional alliance leading to global significance. It is the first Australasian airline system and it will have extremely comprehensive regional rights," he said.

The Ansett tie substantially increased the number of wide-bodied jets available to 35 and makes 86 narrow bodied jets available. It also means access to 29 international airports, 90 Australian airports and 29 New Zealand airports.

In terms of Air NZ's balance sheet, the ratio of net debt to debt debt and equity will go from 16 percent currently, ballooning out to 39 percent post the transaction, and falling back to 28 percent after Air NZ's equity issue.
The impact on earnings would be neutral initially but Air NZ expects it to be revenue-positive in a year.
"It gives the platform going forward to join the global alliance networks of the world, which is how international aviation is moving," McCrea said.
The single aviation market is still on the drawing board, but New Zealand and Australia already enjoy a free market on trans-Tasman routes.
McCrea said Air NZ had pre-emptive rights over News Corp's remaining 50 percent stake in Ansett.
"There is a shareholders' agreement. Naturally, anybody making an investment of this order is going to look after their interests, but that's all I can say."
